c.text: 4 JULY 1054
In China, the emperor's court astronomers saw a new star in the eastern sky at dawn
It was so bright that for 23 days it could be seen even in daylight
A GUEST STAR
About two years later, the guest star faded away
But where it shone, there is now a vast glowing cloud of gas and dust
CRAB NEBULA
About 6,500 light-years away
The guest star was really the death of a massive star...
SUPERNOVA
And in the middle of that explosion, something survived
Something heavier than the Sun, yet only 20 km wide
And it still spins 30 times every second...
NEUTRON STAR
A thousand years later, these stars revealed another secret of the universe: where gold comes from

c.text: NEUTRON
"SUPERNOVA"
The idea of a neutron star was born from a new discovery
In 1932, England's James Chadwick found a new particle inside the atom
It had no electric charge...
Within two years, two astronomers in California connected it to something much bigger
Walter Baade from Germany, and Fritz Zwicky from Switzerland
They wrote that when a massive star explodes, its leftover core can be crushed so hard...
...that its atoms break down into a ball made almost only of neutrons
In the same work, they gave the explosion a name that is still used today...
Most scientists didn't take the idea seriously
A star as small as a city, and heavier than the Sun?
For the next 33 years, nobody saw one

c.text: "SCRUFF"
BAADE AND ZWICKY WERE RIGHT
NOBEL PRIZE 1974
In Cambridge, England, a 24-year-old PhD student, Jocelyn Bell, had built a new radio telescope with her colleagues
It covered as much ground as 57 tennis courts, with more than 2,000 antennas
Every day the telescope printed about 30 metres of chart paper, and Jocelyn read it by hand
In August, she spotted a strange mark on the paper, just half an inch long
She called it...
In November, when the mark was recorded at high speed, it was full of pulses
As regular as the ticking of a clock
One every 1.337 seconds
So regular that the team jokingly named the signal...
LGM-1: "Little Green Men"
But it wasn't aliens. It was the first pulsar
A spinning neutron star that, like a lighthouse, swept a beam of radio waves past Earth on every turn
The very next year, a pulsar was found inside the Crab Nebula too
In 1974, the discovery of pulsars won the Nobel Prize
But not for Jocelyn Bell
It went to her supervisor, Antony Hewish, and to Martin Ryle
44 years later, Jocelyn Bell won a $3 million prize
She gave all of it away, so that students who rarely get the chance could study physics

c.text: Pulsars are such perfect clocks that even the smallest disturbance in their pulses can be caught
In 1990, Polish astronomer Aleksander Wolszczan used the giant Arecibo telescope in Puerto Rico to find a pulsar...
...spinning 161 times a second
Its pulses arrived sometimes a little early, sometimes a little late, in a repeating pattern
Wolszczan and his colleague Dale Frail realised that planets were orbiting the pulsar, tugging on it
The discovery was published in 1992
They were the first confirmed planets around any star other than the Sun
Two planets about four times as heavy as Earth, and later a third, just twice the mass of the Moon
But these planets circle a dead star, under a constant rain of deadly radiation
The first planet around a Sun-like star was found three years later

c.text: TERZAN 5
The strangest thing about neutron stars is how dense they are
When the core of a massive star collapses, more than the Sun's mass is squeezed into a ball just 20 km wide
According to NASA, one teaspoon of neutron star would weigh about a billion tons on Earth
And these balls spin
In 2004, America's Green Bank Telescope recorded a dense cluster of stars called Terzan 5
In that data, McGill University student Jason Hessels found a pulsar spinning 716 times a second
No neutron star has ever been found spinning faster
At that speed, if the star were any bigger, its surface would fly apart
So scientists calculate it can be no more than 32 km across

c.text: MAGNETARS
27 DECEMBER 2004
Some neutron stars have another power. They are the strongest magnets in the universe...
Their magnetic field is about a million billion times stronger than Earth's
27 December 2004
On the far side of the galaxy, tens of thousands of light-years away, the surface of a magnetar suddenly burst
In just a tenth of a second, it released as much energy as the Sun gives off in 150,000 years
The flash was so intense that the detectors of several satellites were blinded for a moment
Its wave even shook the upper layers of Earth's atmosphere
Scientists say that if such a magnetar were within 10 light-years, Earth's atmosphere could have been badly damaged
But after the flash, a faint glow lingered for hours
For 20 years, nobody could explain it

c.text: 17 AUGUST 2017
America's LIGO and Italy's Virgo detectors caught a faint ripple in space
KILONOVA
For about 100 seconds, two neutron stars spiralled closer and closer, and then collided
Just 1.7 seconds later, NASA's Fermi satellite caught a flash of gamma rays from the same direction
Within 11 hours, a telescope in Chile found the crash site...
...in a galaxy 130 million light-years away
Then about 70 observatories turned to look
What they saw had never been seen before
The debris glowed with the light of newly made heavy elements...
It contained platinum. And... gold
By one estimate, this single collision made gold and platinum weighing about ten times as much as Earth

c.text: FAST RADIO BURSTS
28 APRIL 2020
Since 2007, astronomers had been finding strange radio flashes in the sky
Just a millisecond long, but extremely powerful
They came from distant galaxies, and nobody knew what made them. They were named...
28 April 2020
Canada's CHIME telescope, and a few small antennas in California, caught a bright radio flash at the same moment
Those antennas had been built by a Caltech student, Christopher Bochenek
This time, the flash came from inside the Milky Way
It came from a magnetar that was flaring in X-rays at the same time
According to Bochenek, in one millisecond it released as much energy as the Sun does in 30 seconds
A 13-year-old puzzle had its first answer
At least some fast radio bursts come from magnetars

c.text: "BLACK WIDOW"
There is a limit to how heavy a neutron star can be
Any more mass, and it collapses under its own weight into a black hole
Exactly where that limit lies, nobody knows for sure
In 2022, using the Keck telescope in Hawaii, Roger Romani and Alex Filippenko's team measured a strange pair
A pulsar spinning 707 times a second, and its companion star, which it is slowly eating
The companion is now only 20 times as heavy as Jupiter. Pulsars like this are called...
This pulsar weighs 2.35 times as much as the Sun: the heaviest neutron star ever measured
In Filippenko's words, a neutron star is like one giant atomic nucleus

c.text: JUNE 2023
Pulsars are the most perfect clocks in the universe
That gave scientists an amazing idea: turn the whole galaxy into a detector
For 15 years, the NANOGrav team timed the pulses of 68 pulsars across the Milky Way with great precision
If very long gravitational waves were passing through space, the pulsars' ticking would shift in a special pattern
In June 2023, NANOGrav and several other teams around the world showed evidence of exactly that pattern
These waves are years long, and probably come from pairs of giant black holes orbiting each other across the universe

If a magnetar's flash blasts part of its surface into space, heavy elements can form in it
And their radioactive glow would peak about 10 minutes after the flash
Eric Burns of Louisiana State University found exactly such a glow in old data from ESA's INTEGRAL satellite...
